[Biatec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biatec "Biatec"), presumably a king, who appeared on the Celtic coins minted by the [Boii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boii_(Bohemia) "Boii (Bohemia)") at the current location of Bratislava, 1st century B.C.

#### Hallstatt Period

The arrival of tribes from [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace "Thrace") disrupted the people of the Kalenderberg culture, who lived in the hamlets located on the plain ([Sereď](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sere%C4%8F "Sereď")) and in the hill forts like Molpír, near [Smolenice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smolenice "Smolenice"), in the [Little Carpathians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Carpathians "Little Carpathians"). During Hallstatt times, monumental burial mounds were erected in western Slovakia, with princely equipment consisting of richly decorated vessels, ornaments and decorations. The burial rites consisted entirely of cremation. Common people were buried in flat urnfield cemeteries.

A special role was given to weaving and the production of textiles. The local power of the "Princes" of the [Hallstatt period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallstatt_culture "Hallstatt culture") disappeared in Slovakia during the century before the middle of first millennium BCE, after strife between the [Scytho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythians "Scythians")-Thracian people and locals, resulting in abandonment of the old hill-forts. Relatively depopulated areas soon caught the interest of emerging [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts") tribes, who advanced from the south towards the north, following the Slovak rivers, peacefully integrating into the remnants of the local population.

#### La Tène Period

From around 500 BCE, the territory of modern-day Slovakia was settled by [Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celt "Celt"), who built powerful _[oppida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppida "Oppida")_ on the sites of modern-day [Bratislava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava "Bratislava") and [Devín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dev%C3%ADn "Devín"). [Biatecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biatec "Biatec"), [silver coins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_coin "Silver coin") with inscriptions in the Latin alphabet, represent the first known use of writing in Slovakia. At the northern regions, remnants of the local population of Lusatian origin, together with Celtic and later Dacian influence, gave rise to the unique [Púchov culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%BAchov_culture "Púchov culture"), with advanced crafts and iron-working, many hill-forts and fortified settlements of central type with the coinage of the "Velkobysterecky" type (no inscriptions, with a horse on one side and a head on the other). This culture is often connected with the Celtic tribe mentioned in Roman sources as [Cotini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotini "Cotini").

#### Roman Period

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Trencin-Roman2.JPG/250px-Trencin-Roman2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trencin-Roman2.JPG)

A Roman inscription at the castle hill of [Trenčín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tren%C4%8D%C3%ADn "Trenčín") (178–179 AD)

From 2[CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era"), the expanding [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") established and maintained a series of outposts around and just south of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube"), the largest of which were known as [Carnuntum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnuntum "Carnuntum") (whose remains are on the main road halfway between [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") and [Bratislava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava "Bratislava")) and [Brigetio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigetio "Brigetio") (present-day [Szőny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sz%C5%91ny "Szőny") at the Slovak-Hungarian border). Such Roman border settlements were built on the present area of [Rusovce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusovce "Rusovce"), currently a suburb of [Bratislava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava "Bratislava"). The military fort was surrounded by a civilian [vicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicus "Vicus") and several farms of the [villa rustica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_rustica "Villa rustica") type. The name of this settlement was [Gerulata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerulata "Gerulata"). The military fort had an auxiliary cavalry unit, approximately 300 horses strong, modelled after the [Cananefates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cananefates "Cananefates"). The remains of Roman buildings have also survived in [Stupava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stupava,_Slovakia "Stupava, Slovakia"), [Devín Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dev%C3%ADn_Castle "Devín Castle"), Bratislava Castle Hill, and the Bratislava-[Dúbravka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BAbravka,_Bratislava "Dúbravka, Bratislava") suburb.

Near the northernmost line of the Roman hinterlands, the [Limes Romanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limes_Romanus "Limes Romanus"), there existed the winter camp of [Laugaricio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tren%C4%8D%C3%ADn "Trenčín") (modern-day [Trenčín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tren%C4%8D%C3%ADn "Trenčín")) where the Auxiliary of Legion II fought and prevailed in a decisive battle over the Germanic [Quadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadi "Quadi") tribe in 179 CE during the [Marcomannic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcomannic_Wars "Marcomannic Wars"). The Kingdom of [Vannius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannius "Vannius"), a kingdom founded by the [Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_peoples "Germanic peoples")[Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi") tribes of [Quadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadi "Quadi") and [Marcomanni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcomanni "Marcomanni"), as well as several small Germanic and [Celtic tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Celtic_tribes "List of Celtic tribes"), including the Osi and [Cotini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotini "Cotini"), existed in western and central Slovakia from 8–6 BCE to 179 CE.

### Great invasions from the fourth to seventh centuries

In the second and third centuries CE, the [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns "Huns") began to leave the [Central Asian steppes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_Steppe "Eurasian Steppe"). They crossed the Danube in 377 CE and occupied [Pannonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonia "Pannonia"), which they used for 75 years as their base for launching looting-raids into Western Europe. However, [Attila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attila "Attila")'s death in 453 brought about the disappearance of the [Hunnic empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns "Huns"). In 568, a Turko-Mongol tribal confederacy, the [Avars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Avars "Pannonian Avars"), conducted its invasion into the Middle Danube region. The Avars occupied the lowlands of the [Pannonian Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Plain "Pannonian Plain") and established an empire dominating the [Carpathian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Basin "Pannonian Basin").

In 623, the [Slavic population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Slavs "Early Slavs") living in the western parts of Pannonia seceded from their empire after a revolution led by [Samo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samo "Samo"), a Frankish merchant.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-T%C3%B6rt%C3%A9neti_Kronol%C3%B3gia-31) After 626, the Avar power started a gradual decline[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-32) but its reign lasted to 804.

### Avars

In 568, the [Avars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Avars "Pannonian Avars"), under Khagan [Bayan I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayan_I "Bayan I") established an empire in the [Carpathian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Basin "Pannonian Basin") that lasted for 250 years.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-Hun_Avar_Hungarian_Genetics_2019-33)

### Slavic states

The [Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavs "Slavs") tribes settled in the territory of present-day Slovakia in the fifth century. Western Slovakia was the centre of [Samo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samo "Samo")'s empire in the seventh century. A Slavic state known as the [Principality of Nitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Nitra "Principality of Nitra") arose in the eighth century and its ruler [Pribina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pribina "Pribina") had the first known Christian church of the territory of present-day Slovakia consecrated by 828. Together with neighbouring [Moravia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moravia "Moravia"), the principality formed the core of the [Great Moravian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Moravia "Great Moravia") Empire from 833. The high point of this Slavonic empire came with the arrival of [Saints Cyril and Methodius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saints_Cyril_and_Methodius "Saints Cyril and Methodius") in 863, during the reign of [Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke "Duke")[Rastislav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastislav_of_Moravia "Rastislav of Moravia"), and the territorial expansion under [King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King "King")[Svätopluk I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sv%C3%A4topluk_I "Svätopluk I").

#### Great Moravia (830–before 907)

Main article: [Great Moravia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Moravia "Great Moravia")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Cyril_a_metod_zilina.jpg/250px-Cyril_a_metod_zilina.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cyril_a_metod_zilina.jpg)

A statue of [Saint Cyril and Saint Methodius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saints_Cyril_and_Methodius "Saints Cyril and Methodius") in [Žilina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%BDilina "Žilina"). In 863, they introduced [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") to what is now Slovakia.

Great Moravia arose around 830 when [Mojmír I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojmir_I_of_Moravia "Mojmir I of Moravia") unified the [Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavs "Slavs") tribes settled north of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube") and extended the Moravian supremacy over them.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-34) When Mojmír I endeavoured to secede from the supremacy of the king of [East Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia") in 846, King [Louis the German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_the_German "Louis the German") deposed him and assisted Mojmír's nephew [Rastislav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastislav_of_Moravia "Rastislav of Moravia") (846–870) in acquiring the throne.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-Korai_Magyar_T%C3%B6rt%C3%A9neti_Lexikon-35) The new monarch pursued an independent policy: after stopping a Frankish attack in 855, he also sought to weaken the influence of Frankish priests preaching in his realm. [Duke Rastislav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastislav_of_Moravia "Rastislav of Moravia") asked the [Byzantine Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire")[Michael III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_III "Michael III") to send teachers who would interpret Christianity in the Slavic vernacular.

In 862, Prince [Rastislav of Moravia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastislav_of_Moravia "Rastislav of Moravia") rebelled against the [Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks "Franks"), and after hiring [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarians "Hungarians") troops, won his independence; this was the first time that Hungarians expeditionary troops entered the [Carpathian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Basin "Pannonian Basin").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-36)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-37)

On Rastislav's request, two brothers, Byzantine officials and missionaries [Saints Cyril and Methodius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saints_Cyril_and_Methodius "Saints Cyril and Methodius") came in 863. Cyril developed the [first Slavic alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glagolitic_alphabet "Glagolitic alphabet") and translated the Gospel into the [Old Church Slavonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Church_Slavonic "Old Church Slavonic") language. Rastislav was also preoccupied with the security and administration of his state. Numerous fortified castles built throughout the country are dated to his reign and some of them (e.g.,_Dowina_, sometimes identified with [Devín Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dev%C3%ADn_Castle "Devín Castle"))[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-worldarcheology-38)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-caplovic-39) are also mentioned in connection with Rastislav by Frankish chronicles.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-40)[_[full citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources#What\_information\_to\_include "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_][[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-fulda-41)

During Rastislav's reign, the [Principality of Nitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Nitra "Principality of Nitra") was given to his nephew [Svätopluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svatopluk_I_of_Moravia "Svatopluk I of Moravia") as an [appanage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appanage "Appanage").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-caplovic-39) The rebellious prince allied himself with the Franks and overthrew his uncle in 870. Similarly to his predecessor, Svätopluk I (871–894) assumed the title of the king (_rex_). During his reign, the Great Moravian Empire reached its greatest territorial extent, when not only present-day [Moravia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moravia "Moravia") and Slovakia but also present-day northern and [central Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Hungary "Central Hungary"), [Lower Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Austria "Lower Austria"), [Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemia "Bohemia"), [Silesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silesia "Silesia"), [Lusatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusatia "Lusatia"), southern Poland and [northern Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vojvodina "Vojvodina") belonged to the empire, but the exact borders of his domains are still disputed by modern authors.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-T%C3%B3th-42) Svatopluk also withstood attacks of the [Magyar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarians "Hungarians") tribes and the [Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire"), although sometimes it was he who hired the Magyars when waging war against [East Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-43)

In 880, [Pope John VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_VIII "Pope John VIII") set up an independent [ecclesiastical province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_province "Ecclesiastical province") in Great Moravia with Archbishop [Methodius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saints_Cyril_and_Methodius "Saints Cyril and Methodius") as its head. He also named the German cleric [Wiching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiching "Wiching") the bishop of [Nitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitra "Nitra").

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Great_Moravia.svg/250px-Great_Moravia.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Great_Moravia.svg)

Certain and disputed borders of Great Moravia under [Svatopluk I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svatopluk_I_of_Moravia "Svatopluk I of Moravia") (according to modern historians)

After the death of Prince Svatopluk in 894, his sons [Mojmír II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojmir_II_of_Moravia "Mojmir II of Moravia") (894–906?) and [Svatopluk II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svatopluk_II "Svatopluk II") succeeded him as the Prince of Great Moravia and the Prince of Nitra respectively.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-caplovic-39) However, they started to quarrel for domination of the whole empire. Weakened by an internal conflict as well as by constant warfare with [Eastern Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Francia "Eastern Francia"), Great Moravia lost most of its peripheral territories.

It is not known what happened with both Mojmír II and Svatopluk II because they are not mentioned in written sources after 906. In [three battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Pressburg "Battle of Pressburg") (4–5 July and 9 August 907) near [Bratislava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava "Bratislava"), the Magyars routed [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria") armies. Some historians put this year as the date of the break-up of the Great Moravian Empire, due to the Hungarian conquest; other historians take the date a little bit earlier (to 902).

Great Moravia left behind a lasting legacy in Central and Eastern Europe. The [Glagolitic script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glagolitic_alphabet "Glagolitic alphabet") and its successor [Cyrillic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script "Cyrillic script") were disseminated to other Slavic countries, charting a new path in their [sociocultural development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociocultural_evolution "Sociocultural evolution").

### Grand Principality of Hungary (895–1000)

Main article: [Principality of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Hungary "Principality of Hungary")

Foundation of the [Hungarian state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Hungary "Principality of Hungary") is connected to the [Hungarian conquerors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_conquest_of_the_Carpathian_Basin "Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin"), who arrived from the [Pontic steppes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontic%E2%80%93Caspian_steppe "Pontic–Caspian steppe") as a confederation of [seven tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_chieftains_of_the_Magyars "Seven chieftains of the Magyars"). The [Hungarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarians "Hungarians") arrived in the frame of a strong centralized steppe-empire under the leadership of Grand Prince [Álmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81lmos "Álmos") and his son [Árpád](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d "Árpád"), they became founders of the [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty"), the Hungarian ruling dynasty and the Hungarian state. The [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty") claimed to be a direct descendant of the great Hun leader Attila.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-44)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-45)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-46) The [Hungarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarians "Hungarians") took possession of the [Carpathian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Basin "Pannonian Basin") in a pre-planned manner, with a long move-in between 862 and 895.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-47) Their armies' advance may have been promoted by continuous wars among the countries of the region whose rulers still hired them occasionally to intervene in their struggles.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-Krist%C3%B3_2-48)

Just a few decades after the collapse of the [Avar Khaganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Avars "Pannonian Avars") in 822, once again a steppe empire, the Hungarian Grand Principality united the Carpathian Basin under its rule. Only the [East Frankish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia") had such military power that it could intervent in the formation of the new order. His leadership also wanted to eliminate the new steppe state because the East Frankish Empire lost Pannonia and its Christian Avar taxpayers, and his territory was hit by increasing attacks by the Hungarians, especially Bavaria, which was then the eastern province of the Eastern Frankish Kingdom. In 907, three East Francian armies led by [Luitpold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luitpold,_Margrave_of_Bavaria "Luitpold, Margrave of Bavaria"), Margrave of Bavaria, which entered the Hungarian territory in order to expel the Hungarians from the Carpathian Basin, is annihilated by the Hungarian army at the [Battle of Pressburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Pressburg "Battle of Pressburg"). Luitpold, Margrave of Bavaria, Dietmar I, Archbishop of Salzburg, Prince Sieghard, 19 counts, 2 bishops, and 3 abbots are killed in the battle, together with the majority of the soldiers. The Hungarians secured the lands they gained during the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin, and prevented a future German invasion, the Germans did not launch an imperial scale campaign against Hungary for 123 years until 1030.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-Szabados_-_Battle_of_Pressburg_2023-49)

### The Kingdom of Hungary, the Habsburg Monarchy and the Ottoman Empire (1000–1918)

Main articles: [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary "Kingdom of Hungary"), [Habsburg monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy"), and [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/K%C3%A9pes_kr%C3%B3nika_-_39.oldal_-_Istv%C3%A1n_kir%C3%A1ly_hadi_d%C3%ADszben.jpg/250px-K%C3%A9pes_kr%C3%B3nika_-_39.oldal_-_Istv%C3%A1n_kir%C3%A1ly_hadi_d%C3%ADszben.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:K%C3%A9pes_kr%C3%B3nika_-_39.oldal_-_Istv%C3%A1n_kir%C3%A1ly_hadi_d%C3%ADszben.jpg)

[Stephen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_I_of_Hungary "Stephen I of Hungary"), [King of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Hungary "King of Hungary")

In 972, the ruling prince [Géza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A9za,_Grand_Prince_of_the_Hungarians "Géza, Grand Prince of the Hungarians") of the [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty") officially started to integrate [Grand Principality of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Hungary "Principality of Hungary") into Christian Western Europe. His son [Saint Stephen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_I_of_Hungary "Stephen I of Hungary") became the first [King of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Hungary "King of Hungary") after defeating his [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paganism "Paganism") uncle [Koppány](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kopp%C3%A1ny "Koppány"). Under Stephen, Hungary was recognised as a Catholic [Apostolic Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_Majesty "Apostolic Majesty"). Applying to [Pope Sylvester II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Sylvester_II "Pope Sylvester II"), Stephen received the insignia of royalty (including probably a part of the [Holy Crown of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Crown_of_Hungary "Holy Crown of Hungary")) from the papacy.

In the years 1001–1002 and 1018–1029, Slovakia was part of the [Kingdom of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Poland "Kingdom of Poland"), having been conquered by [Boleslaus I the Brave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleslaus_I_the_Brave "Boleslaus I the Brave").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-50) After the territory of Slovakia was returned to Hungary, a semi-autonomous polity continued to exist (or was created in 1048 by king [Andrew I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_I_of_Hungary "Andrew I of Hungary")) called [Duchy of Nitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Nitra "Duchy of Nitra"). Comprising roughly the territory of [Principality of Nitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Nitra "Principality of Nitra") and [Bihar principality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar_County "Bihar County"), they formed what was called a _tercia pars regni_, third of a kingdom.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-51)

This polity existed up until 1108/1110, after which it was not restored. After this, up until the collapse of [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") in 1918, the territory of Slovakia was an integral part of the Hungarian state.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-52)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-53)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-54) The ethnic composition of Slovakia became more diverse with the arrival of the [Carpathian Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Germans "Carpathian Germans") in the 13th century and the [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") in the 14th century.

A significant decline in the population resulted from the [invasion of the Mongols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Europe "Mongol invasion of Europe") in 1241 and the subsequent famine. After the invasion, much of the territory was destroyed, but was recovered largely thanks to Hungarian king [Béla IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_IV_of_Hungary "Béla IV of Hungary"). However, in medieval times the area of Slovakia was characterised by German and [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") immigration, burgeoning towns, construction of numerous stone castles, and the cultivation of the arts.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-tibensky-55) The arrival of German element sometimes proved a problem for the autochthonous Slovaks (and even Hungarians in the broader Hungary), since they often quickly gained most power in medieval towns, only to later refuse to share it. Breaking of old customs by Germans often resulted in national quarrels. One of which had to be sorted out by the king [Louis I.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I_of_Hungary "Louis I of Hungary") with the proclamation [Privilegium pro Slavis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privilegium_pro_Slavis "Privilegium pro Slavis") (Privilege for Slovaks) in the year 1381. According to this privilege, Slovaks and [Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Germans "Carpathian Germans") were to occupy each half of the seats in the city council of [Žilina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%BDilina "Žilina") and the mayor should be elected each year, alternating between those nationalities. This would not be the last such case.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-56)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/1franci2.jpg/250px-1franci2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1franci2.jpg)

One of the commanders of a Slovak volunteers' army captain [Ján Francisci-Rimavský](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A1n_Francisci-Rimavsk%C3%BD "Ján Francisci-Rimavský") during the [fight for independence from the Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovak_Uprising_of_1848%E2%80%9349 "Slovak Uprising of 1848–49")

In 1465, King [Matthias Corvinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthias_Corvinus_of_Hungary "Matthias Corvinus of Hungary") founded the Hungarian Kingdom's third university, in Pressburg ([Bratislava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava "Bratislava")), but it was closed in 1490 after his death.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-57)[Hussites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussites "Hussites") also settled in the region after the [Hussite Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite_Wars "Hussite Wars").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-books.google.pl-58)

Owing to the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire")'s expansion into Hungarian territory, [Bratislava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava "Bratislava") was designated the new capital of Hungary in 1536, ahead of the fall of the old Hungarian capital of [Buda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buda "Buda") in 1541. It became part of the Austrian Habsburg monarchy, marking the beginning of a new era. The territory comprising modern Slovakia, then known as [Upper Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Hungary "Upper Hungary"), became the place of settlement for nearly two-thirds of the [Magyar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyar_tribes "Magyar tribes") nobility fleeing the Turks and became far more linguistically and culturally Hungarian than it was before.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-books.google.pl-58) Partly thanks to old [Hussite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite "Hussite") families and Slovaks studying under [Martin Luther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther "Martin Luther"), the region then experienced a growth in [Protestantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-books.google.pl-58) For a short period in the 17th century, most Slovaks were [Lutherans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutherans "Lutherans").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-books.google.pl-58) They defied the Catholic Habsburgs and sought protection from neighbouring [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania"), a rival continuation of the [Magyar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyar_tribes "Magyar tribes") state that practised religious tolerance and normally had Ottoman backing. Upper Hungary, modern Slovakia, became the site of frequent wars between Catholics in the west territory and Protestants in the east, as well as against Turks; the frontier was on a constant state of military alert and heavily fortified by castles and citadels often manned by Catholic German and Slovak troops on the Habsburg side. By 1648, Slovakia was not spared the [Counter-Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-Reformation "Counter-Reformation"), which brought the majority of its population from Lutheranism back to [Roman Catholicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholicism "Roman Catholicism"). In 1655, the printing press at the [Trnava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trnava "Trnava") university produced the Jesuit Benedikt Szöllősi's Cantus Catholici, a Catholic hymnal in Slovak that reaffirmed links to the earlier works of Cyril and Methodius.

The [Ottoman wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_wars_in_Europe "Ottoman wars in Europe"), the rivalry between Austria and [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania"), and the frequent insurrections against the [Habsburg monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy") inflicted a great deal of devastation, especially in the rural areas.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-59) In the [Austro-Turkish War (1663–1664)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Turkish_War_(1663%E2%80%931664) "Austro-Turkish War (1663–1664)") a Turkish army led by the [Grand Vizier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Vizier "Grand Vizier") decimated Slovakia.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-books.google.pl-58) In 1682, the [Principality of Upper Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Upper_Hungary "Principality of Upper Hungary"), a short-lived Ottoman vassal state, was established in the territory of modern Slovakia. Prior to this, regions on its southern rim were already encompassed in the [Egri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E%C4%9Fri_Eyalet "Eğri Eyalet"), [Budin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budin_Eyalet "Budin Eyalet") and [Uyvar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyvar_Eyalet "Uyvar Eyalet")[eyalets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyalet "Eyalet").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-Pirick%C3%BD-2023-16)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-60)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-%C3%81goston-1998-17)[Thököly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emeric_Th%C3%B6k%C3%B6ly "Emeric Thököly")'s [kuruc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuruc "Kuruc") rebels from the Principality of Upper Hungary fought alongside the Turks against the Austrians and Poles at the [Battle of Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vienna "Battle of Vienna") of 1683 led by [John III Sobieski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III_Sobieski "John III Sobieski"). As the [Turks withdrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Turkish_War "Great Turkish War") from Hungary in the late 17th century, the importance of the territory composing modern Slovakia decreased, although [Pressburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressburg "Pressburg") retained its status as the capital of Hungary until 1848 when it was transferred back to Buda.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-61)

During the [revolution of 1848–49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1848_in_the_Habsburg_areas "Revolutions of 1848 in the Habsburg areas"), the [Slovaks started uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovak_Volunteer_Campaigns "Slovak Volunteer Campaigns"), supporting the [Austrian Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_of_Austria "Emperor of Austria"), hoping for independence from the Hungarian part of the [Dual Monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") and greater autonomy within the empire. They failed to achieve their aim, but the conflict resulted in Slovak rights for language in certain administrative and educational areas.

Thereafter, relations between the nationalities deteriorated (see [Magyarisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyarisation "Magyarisation")), culminating in the secession of Slovakia from Hungary after World War I.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia#cite_note-62)

The [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU) is a [supranational union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supranational_union "Supranational union") of 27 member states that are party to the EU's [founding treaties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaties_of_the_European_Union "Treaties of the European Union"), and thereby subject to the privileges and obligations of membership. They have agreed by the treaties to share their own sovereignty through the [institutions of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutions_of_the_European_Union "Institutions of the European Union") in certain aspects of government. State governments must agree unanimously in the [Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_the_European_Union "Council of the European Union") for the union to adopt some policies; for others, collective decisions are made by [qualified majority voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_in_the_Council_of_the_European_Union "Voting in the Council of the European Union"). These obligations and sharing of sovereignty (also known by some as "pooling of sovereignty") within the EU make it unique among international organisations, as it has established its own legal order which by the provisions of the founding treaties is [both legally binding and supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primacy_of_European_Union_law "Primacy of European Union law") on all the member states (after [a landmark ruling of the ECJ in 1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_v_ENEL "Costa v ENEL")). A founding principle of the union is [subsidiarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidiarity_(European_Union) "Subsidiarity (European Union)"), meaning that decisions are taken collectively if and only if they cannot realistically be taken individually.

Each member country appoints to the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") a [European commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_commissioner "European commissioner"). The commissioners do not represent their member state, but instead work collectively in the interests of all the member states within the EU.

In the 1950s, [six core states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Six "Inner Six") founded the EU's predecessor [European Communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Communities "European Communities") ([Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), and [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany")). The remaining states have acceded in subsequent [enlargements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_European_Union "Enlargement of the European Union"). To accede, a state must fulfil the economic and political requirements known as the [Copenhagen criteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen_criteria "Copenhagen criteria"), which require a candidate to have a democratic government and [free-market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_market "Free market") together with the corresponding freedoms and institutions, and respect for the [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law"). Enlargement of the Union is also contingent upon the consent of all existing members and the candidate's adoption of the existing body of EU law, known as the _[acquis communautaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquis\_communautaire "Acquis communautaire")_.

The [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), which had acceded to the EU's predecessor in 1973, ceased to be an EU member state on 31 January 2020, in a political process known as [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit"). No other member state has withdrawn from the EU and none has been suspended, although some dependent territories or semi-autonomous areas have left.

## Abbreviations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_state_of_the_European_Union&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Abbreviations")]

[Abbreviations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbreviation "Abbreviation") have been used as a shorthand way of grouping countries by their date of accession.

*   **EU15** includes the fifteen countries in the European Union from 1 January 1995 to 30 April 2004. The EU15 comprised Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and United Kingdom.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-32)[Eurostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurostat "Eurostat") still uses this expression.
*   **EU19** includes the countries in the EU15 as well as the [Central European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Europe "Central Europe") member countries of the OECD: Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovak Republic.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-33)
*   **EU11** is used to refer to the Central, [Southeastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Europe "Southeastern Europe") and [Baltic European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_states "Baltic states") member states that joined in 2004, 2007 and 2013: in 2004 the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, the Slovak Republic, and Slovenia; in 2007 Bulgaria, Romania; and in 2013 Croatia.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-34)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-35)
*   **EU27** means all the member states. It was originally used in this sense from 2007 until Croatia's accession in 2013, and during the [Brexit negotiations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_negotiations "Brexit negotiations") from 2017 until the United Kingdom's withdrawal on 31 January 2020 it came to mean all members except the UK.
*   **EU28** meant all the member states from the accession of Croatia in 2013 to the withdrawal of the United Kingdom in 2020.

Additionally, other abbreviations have been used to refer to countries which [had limited access to the EU labour market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_movement_for_workers_in_the_European_Union#Summary "Freedom of movement for workers in the European Union").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-36)

*   [A8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A8_countries "A8 countries") is eight of the ten countries that joined the EU in 2004, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, the Slovak Republic, and Slovenia.
*   A2 is the countries that joined the EU in 2007, Bulgaria and Romania.

Member states of the European Union (dark blue) (1993–present). Pre-1993, the EU was known as the European Communities (sky blue). Animated in order of accession and secession.

According to the [Copenhagen criteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen_criteria "Copenhagen criteria"), membership of the European Union is open to any European country that is a stable, [free-market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_market "Free market")[liberal democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_democracy "Liberal democracy") that respects the [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law") and human rights. Furthermore, it has to be willing to accept all the obligations of membership, such as adopting all previously agreed law (the 170,000 pages of [acquis communautaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquis_communautaire "Acquis communautaire")) and switching to the [euro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-37) For a state to join the European Union, the prior approval of all current member states is required. In addition to enlargement by adding new countries, the EU can also expand by having territories of member states, which are outside the EU, integrate more closely (for example in respect to the [dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Netherlands_Antilles "Dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles")) or by a territory of a member state which had previously seceded and then rejoined (see withdrawal below).

### Suspension

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_state_of_the_European_Union&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Suspension")]

Main article: [Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_7_of_the_Treaty_on_European_Union "Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union")

There is no provision to expel a member state, but [TEU Article 7](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Consolidated%20version%20of%20the%20Treaty%20on%20European%20Union/Title%20I:%20Common%20Provisions#Article_7 "s:Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union/Title I: Common Provisions") provides for the suspension of certain rights. Introduced in the [Treaty of Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Amsterdam "Treaty of Amsterdam"), Article 7 outlines that if a member persistently breaches the EU's founding principles (liberty, democracy, human rights and so forth, outlined in [TEU Article 2](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Consolidated%20version%20of%20the%20Treaty%20on%20European%20Union/Title%20I:%20Common%20Provisions#Article_2 "s:Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union/Title I: Common Provisions")) then the [European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council "European Council") can vote to suspend any rights of membership, such as voting and representation. Identifying the breach requires unanimity (excluding the state concerned), but sanctions require only a qualified majority.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-suspend-38)

The state in question would still be bound by the obligations treaties and the Council acting by majority may alter or lift such sanctions. The [Treaty of Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Nice "Treaty of Nice") included a preventive mechanism whereby the council, acting by majority, may identify a potential breach and make recommendations to the state to rectify it before action is taken against it as outlined above.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-suspend-38) However, the treaties do not provide any mechanism to expel a member state outright.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-expel-39)

### Withdrawal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_state_of_the_European_Union&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Withdrawal")]

Main article: [Withdrawal from the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_from_the_European_Union "Withdrawal from the European Union")

Prior to the [Lisbon Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Treaty "Lisbon Treaty"), there was no provision or procedure within any of the [Treaties of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaties_of_the_European_Union "Treaties of the European Union") for a member state to withdraw from the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") or its predecessor organisations. The Lisbon Treaty changed this and included the first provision and procedure of a member state to leave the bloc. The procedure for a state to leave is outlined in [TEU Article 50](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Consolidated%20version%20of%20the%20Treaty%20on%20European%20Union/Title%20VI:%20Final%20Provisions#Article_50 "s:Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union/Title VI: Final Provisions") which also makes clear that "Any Member State may decide to withdraw from the Union in accordance with its own constitutional requirements". Although it calls for a negotiated withdrawal between the seceding state and the rest of the EU, if no agreement is reached two years after the seceding state notifying of its intention to leave, it would cease to be subject to the treaties anyway (thus ensuring a right to unilateral withdrawal).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-expel-39) There is no formal limit to how much time a member state can take between adopting a policy of withdrawal, and actually triggering Article 50.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In a [referendum in June 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum"), the United Kingdom voted to withdraw from the EU. The UK government triggered Article 50 on 29 March 2017.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-GuardianMay-40) After an extended period of negotiation and internal political debate the UK eventually withdrew from the EU on 31 January 2020.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-41)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-42)

Prior to 2016, no member state had voted to withdraw. However, [French Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Algeria "French Algeria"), [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland") and [Saint-Barthélemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Barth%C3%A9lemy "Saint-Barthélemy") did cease being part of the EU (or its predecessor) in 1962, 1985, and 2012, respectively, due to status changes. The situation of Greenland being outside the EU while still subject to an EU member state had been discussed as a template for the pro-EU regions of the UK remaining within the EU or its single market.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-43)

Beyond the formal withdrawal of a member state, there are a number of independence movements such as [Catalonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_independentism "Catalan independentism") or [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothetical_partition_of_Belgium "Hypothetical partition of Belgium") which could result in a situation similar to Greenland's. Were a territory of a member state to secede but wish to remain in the EU, some scholars claim it would need to reapply to join as if it were a new country applying from scratch.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-44) However, other studies claim internal enlargement is legally viable if, in case of a member state dissolution or secession, the resulting states are _all_ considered [successor states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_of_states "Succession of states").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-45) There is also a [European Citizens' Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Citizens'_Initiative "European Citizens' Initiative") that aims at guaranteeing the continuity of rights and obligations of the European citizens belonging to a new state arising from the democratic secession of a European Union member state.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-46)

## Representation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_state_of_the_European_Union&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Representation")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Familiefoto_europese_raad_2011.jpg/500px-Familiefoto_europese_raad_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Familiefoto_europese_raad_2011.jpg)

A 2011 'family photo' of the [European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council "European Council"), which comprises the [heads of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state "Head of state") or [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government "Head of government") of the member states, along with [President of the European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_European_Council "President of the European Council") and the [President of the European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_European_Commission "President of the European Commission")

Each state has representation in the [institutions of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutions_of_the_European_Union "Institutions of the European Union"). Full membership gives the government of a member state a seat in the [Council of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_the_European_Union "Council of the European Union") and [European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council "European Council"). When decisions are not being taken by [consensus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_decision-making "Consensus decision-making"), [qualified majority voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualified_majority_voting "Qualified majority voting") (which requires majorities both of the number of states and of the population they represent, but a sufficient [blocking minority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_in_the_Council_of_the_European_Union "Voting in the Council of the European Union") can veto the proposal). The [Presidency of the Council of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_the_Council_of_the_European_Union "Presidency of the Council of the European Union") rotates among each of the member states, allowing each state six months to help direct the agenda of the EU.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-47)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-48)

Similarly, each state is assigned [seats in Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_European_Parliament "Member of the European Parliament") according to their population (smaller countries receiving more seats per inhabitant than the larger ones). The members of the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") have been elected by [universal suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_suffrage "Universal suffrage") since 1979 (before that, they were seconded from [national parliaments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parliaments_of_the_European_Union "National parliaments of the European Union")).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-49)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-50)

The national governments appoint one member each to the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission"), the [European Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Justice "European Court of Justice") and the [European Court of Auditors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Auditors "European Court of Auditors"). Prospective Commissioners must be confirmed both by the President of the Commission and by the European Parliament; prospective justices must be confirmed by the existing members. Historically, larger member states were granted an extra Commissioner. However, as the body grew, this right has been removed and each state is represented equally. The six largest states are also granted an Advocates General in the Court of Justice. Finally, the Governing Council of the [European Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank "European Central Bank") includes the governors of the national central banks (who may or may not be government appointed) of each [euro area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone") country.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-51)

The larger states traditionally carry more weight in negotiations, however smaller states can be effective impartial mediators and citizens of smaller states are often appointed to sensitive top posts to avoid competition between the larger states. This, together with the disproportionate representation of the smaller states in terms of votes and seats in parliament, gives the smaller EU states a greater power of influence than is normally attributed to a state of their size. However most negotiations are still dominated by the larger states. This has traditionally been largely through the "[Franco-German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France%E2%80%93Germany_relations "France–Germany relations") motor" but Franco-German influence has diminished slightly following the [influx of new members in 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_enlargement_of_the_European_Union "2004 enlargement of the European Union") (see [G6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G6_(EU) "G6 (EU)")).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-52)

## Sovereignty

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_state_of_the_European_Union&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sovereignty")]

Article 4

> 1.   In accordance with Article 5, competences not conferred upon the Union in the Treaties remain with the member states.
> 2.   The Union shall respect the equality of member states before the Treaties as well as their national identities, inherent in their fundamental structures, political and constitutional, inclusive of regional and local self-government. It shall respect their essential State functions, including ensuring the territorial integrity of the State, maintaining law and order and safeguarding national security. In particular, national security remains the sole responsibility of each member state.
> 3.   Pursuant to the principle of [sincere cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sincere_cooperation "Sincere cooperation"), the Union and the member states shall, in full mutual respect, assist each other in carrying out tasks which flow from the Treaties. The member states shall take any appropriate measure, general or particular, to ensure fulfilment of the obligations arising out of the Treaties or resulting from the acts of the institutions of the Union. The member states shall facilitate the achievement of the Union's tasks and refrain from any measure which could jeopardise the attainment of the Union's objectives.

—[Article 4 of the Treaty on European Union](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Consolidated%20version%20of%20the%20Treaty%20on%20European%20Union/Title%20I:%20Common%20Provisions#Article_4 "s:Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union/Title I: Common Provisions")

While the member states are sovereign, the union partially follows a [supranational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supranational_union "Supranational union") system for those functions agreed by treaty to be shared. ("Competences not conferred upon the Union in the Treaties remain with the member states"). Previously limited to [European Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Community "European Community") matters, the practice, known as the '[community method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_method "Community method")', is currently used in many areas of policy. _Combined sovereignty_ is delegated by each member to the institutions in return for representation within those institutions. This practice is often referred to as 'pooling of sovereignty'. Those institutions are then empowered to make laws and execute them at a European level.

In contrast to some international organisations, the EU's style of integration as a [union of states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_union "Political union") does not "emphasise sovereignty or the separation of domestic and foreign affairs [and it] has become a highly developed system for mutual interference in each other's domestic affairs, right down to beer and sausages.".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-53) However, on defence and foreign policy issues (and, pre-[Lisbon Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Treaty "Lisbon Treaty"), police and judicial matters) less sovereignty is transferred, with issues being dealt with by unanimity and co-operation. Very early on in the history of the EU, the unique state of its establishment and pooling of sovereignty was emphasised by the Court of Justice:[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-54)

> By creating a Community of unlimited duration, having its own institutions, its own personality, its own legal capacity and capacity of representation on the international plane and, more particularly, real powers stemming from a limitation of sovereignty or a transfer of powers from the States to Community, the Member States have limited their sovereign rights and have thus created a body of law which binds both their nationals and themselves...The transfer by the States from their domestic legal system to the Community legal system of the rights and obligations arising under the Treaty carries with it a permanent limitation of their sovereign rights.

—[European Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Justice "European Court of Justice") 1964, in reference to case of [Costa v ENEL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_v_ENEL "Costa v ENEL")[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-55)

The question of [whether Union law is superior to State law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supremacy_(European_Union_law) "Supremacy (European Union law)") is subject to some debate. The treaties do not give a judgement on the matter but court judgements have established EU's law superiority over national law and it is affirmed in a declaration attached to the Treaty of Lisbon (the proposed [European Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Constitution "European Constitution") would have fully enshrined this). The legal systems of some states also explicitly accept the Court of Justice's interpretation, such as France and Italy, however in Poland it does not override the [state's constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Republic_of_Poland "Constitution of the Republic of Poland"), which it does in Germany.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-56)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-57) The exact areas where the member states have given legislative competence to the Union are as follows. Every area not mentioned remains with member states.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-58)

### Conditional mutual support

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_state_of_the_European_Union&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Conditional mutual support")]

Due to the [Euro area crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_area_crisis "Euro area crisis"), some [eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone") states were given a [bailout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailout "Bailout") from their fellow members via the [European Financial Stability Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Financial_Stability_Facility "European Financial Stability Facility") and [European Financial Stability Mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Financial_Stability_Mechanism "European Financial Stability Mechanism") (replaced by the [European Stability Mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Stability_Mechanism "European Stability Mechanism") from 2013), but this came with conditions. As a result of the [Greek government-debt crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_government-debt_crisis "Greek government-debt crisis"), Greece accepted a large austerity plan including privatisations and a sell off of state assets in exchange for their bailout. To ensure that Greece complied with the conditions set by the [European troika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_troika "European troika") (ECB, IMF, Commission), a 'large-scale technical assistance' from the European Commission and other member states was deployed to Greek government ministries. Some, including the [President of the Euro Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_Group#President "Euro Group")[Jean-Claude Juncker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Juncker "Jean-Claude Juncker"), stated that "the sovereignty of Greece will be massively limited."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-60)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-61)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-protectorate-62) The situation of the bailed out countries (Greece, Portugal and Ireland) has been described as being a [ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward_(law) "Ward (law)")[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-63)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-64) or [protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate")[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-protectorate-62)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-65)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-66) of the EU with some such as the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") calling for a formalisation of the situation.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-67)

## Multi-speed integration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_state_of_the_European_Union&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Multi-speed integration")]

Main article: [European integration §Multi-speed Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_integration#Multi-speed_Europe "European integration")

See also: [Enhanced cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_cooperation "Enhanced cooperation") and [Opt-outs in the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opt-outs_in_the_European_Union "Opt-outs in the European Union")

EU integration is not always symmetrical, with some states proceeding with integration ahead of hold-outs. There are several different forms of closer integration both within and outside the EU's normal framework. One mechanism is [enhanced cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_cooperation "Enhanced cooperation") where nine or more states can use EU structures to progress in a field that not all states are willing to partake in.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-68) Some states have gained an [opt-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opt-outs_in_the_European_Union "Opt-outs in the European Union") in the founding treaties from participating in certain policy areas.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-69)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-70)

For a more comprehensive list, see [List of European Union member states by political system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_Union_member_states_by_political_system "List of European Union member states by political system").

The admission of a new state the Union is limited to liberal democracies and [Freedom House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House "Freedom House") ranks all EU states as being totally free electoral democracies.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-71) All but 4 are ranked at the top 1.0 rating.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-72) However, the exact political system of a state is not limited, with each state having its own system based on its historical evolution.

More than half of member states—16 out of 27—are [parliamentary republics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_republic "Parliamentary republic"), while six states are [constitutional monarchies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy"), meaning they have a monarch although political powers are exercised by elected politicians. Most republics and all the monarchies operate a [parliamentary system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_system "Parliamentary system") whereby the head of state (president or monarch) has a largely ceremonial role with [reserve powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_power "Reserve power"). That means most power is in the hands of what is called in most of those countries the prime minister, who is accountable to the [national parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parliaments_of_the_European_Union "National parliaments of the European Union"). Of the remaining republics, four[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] operate a [semi-presidential system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-presidential_system "Semi-presidential system"), where competences are shared between the president and prime minister, while one republic operates a [presidential system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_system "Presidential system"), where the president is head of both state and government.

Parliamentary structure in member states varies: there are 15 [unicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicameral "Unicameral") national parliaments and 12 [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameralism "Bicameralism") parliaments. The prime minister and government are usually directly accountable to the directly elected [lower house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_house "Lower house") and require its support to stay in office—the exception being Cyprus with its presidential system. [Upper houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_house "Upper house") are composed differently in different member states: it can be directly elected like the [Polish senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Poland "Senate of Poland"); indirectly elected, for example, by regional legislatures like the [Federal Council of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Council_of_Austria "Federal Council of Austria"); or unelected, but representing certain interest groups like the [National Council of Slovenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_of_Slovenia "National Council of Slovenia"). All elections in member states use some form of [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation"). The most common type of proportional representation is the [party-list system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party-list_proportional_representation "Party-list proportional representation").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

There are also differences in the level of [self-governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governance "Self-governance") for the sub-regions of a member state. Most states, especially the smaller ones, are [unitary states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state "Unitary state"); meaning all major political power is concentrated at the national level. 9 states allocate power to more local levels of government. Austria, Belgium and Germany are full federations, meaning their regions have constitutional autonomies. Denmark, Finland, France and the Netherlands are [federacies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federacy "Federacy"), meaning some regions have autonomy but most do not. Spain and Italy have systems of [devolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devolution "Devolution") where regions have autonomy, but the national government retains the legal right to revoke it.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union#cite_note-73)

States such as France have a number of [overseas territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Member_State_territories_and_the_European_Union "Special Member State territories and the European Union"), retained from their [former empires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_empire "Colonial empire").

The [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU) is a [supranational union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supranational_union "Supranational union") of 27 member states that are party to the EU's [founding treaties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaties_of_the_European_Union "Treaties of the European Union"), and thereby subject to the privileges and obligations of membership. They have agreed by the treaties to share their own sovereignty through the [institutions of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutions_of_the_European_Union "Institutions of the European Union") in certain aspects of government. State governments must agree unanimously in the [Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_the_European_Union "Council of the European Union") for the union to adopt some policies; for others, collective decisions are made by [qualified majority voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_in_the_Council_of_the_European_Union "Voting in the Council of the European Union"). These obligations and sharing of sovereignty (also known by some as "pooling of sovereignty") within the EU make it unique among international organisations, as it has established its own legal order which by the provisions of the founding treaties is [both legally binding and supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primacy_of_European_Union_law "Primacy of European Union law") on all the member states (after [a landmark ruling of the ECJ in 1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_v_ENEL "Costa v ENEL")). A founding principle of the union is [subsidiarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidiarity_(European_Union) "Subsidiarity (European Union)"), meaning that decisions are taken collectively if and only if they cannot realistically be taken individually.

Each member country appoints to the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") a [European commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_commissioner "European commissioner"). The commissioners do not represent their member state, but instead work collectively in the interests of all the member states within the EU.

In the 1950s, [six core states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Six "Inner Six") founded the EU's predecessor [European Communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Communities "European Communities") ([Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), and [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany")). The remaining states have acceded in subsequent [enlargements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_European_Union "Enlargement of the European Union"). To accede, a state must fulfil the economic and political requirements known as the [Copenhagen criteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen_criteria "Copenhagen criteria"), which require a candidate to have a democratic government and [free-market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_market "Free market") together with the corresponding freedoms and institutions, and respect for the [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law"). Enlargement of the Union is also contingent upon the consent of all existing members and the candidate's adoption of the existing body of EU law, known as the _[acquis communautaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquis\_communautaire "Acquis communautaire")_.

The [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), which had acceded to the EU's predecessor in 1973, ceased to be an EU member state on 31 January 2020, in a political process known as [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit"). No other member state has withdrawn from the EU and none has been suspended, although some dependent territories or semi-autonomous areas have left.
